title: How ProWein 2027 Is Looking to the Future of Wine
summary:
The annual trade fair in Düsseldorf is back, March 7 to 9, with engaging seminars, nights on the town, and lots of opportunities to discover new wines.

The post How ProWein 2027 Is Looking to the Future of Wine appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
From March 7 to 9, thousands of wine industry pros will descend upon Messe Düsseldorf’s fairgrounds, eager to discover wine’s new frontiers at the 2027 ProWein International Trade Fair. For 30 years, ProWein has served as a seminal congregation of buyers and suppliers from all over the world, and this year’s edition is expected to welcome trade professionals from over 140 countries for spirited seminars, curated tastings, and eclectic activations.

To get the scoop on what will set ProWein 2027 apart from previous iterations—and what’s next for the wine industry—we caught up with the fair’s director, Frank Schindler.

What do you think will be the most discussed topics at ProWein 2027?

“Given the current backdrop of social, economic, and political upheaval, I would highlight three topics that will be on the minds of our exhibitors and partners—starting with how they can ensure their own success and profitability. Especially in challenging times, a trade fair must specifically lead to new orders and revenue streams. That is the rationale behind our Hosted Buyer Program, where we target key buyers from Germany, the United Kingdom, Benelux, Eastern Europe, Scandinavia, and Austria, plus top buyers from Asia, Africa, and the Americas.

I believe the second topic is ‘what changes need to be made to product lineup/markets’ in light of trends such as the increasing popularity of ‘no-and-low’ beverages. That’s where we really see a role for our Agora format, a focused three-day program where international industry representatives will meet with experts from other fields to discuss trends, market analyses, business insights, and strategic perspectives.

And lastly, but no less important, is new trends or discoveries so our visitors and partners leave with an awareness of new products or categories that help them in their business. That’s what our new Discovery Zone is targeting in particular because it offers younger, smaller businesses a cost-efficient format to connect with an international audience of buyers and partners.”

Last year’s event introduced ProWein City Vibes. How was the nighttime event series received? Why was involving the city, people, and nightlife of Düsseldorf important?

“There are far more wine lovers in Düsseldorf than one might expect from a city that used to be known for its beer drinking. This, of course, poses a significant challenge to our strict ‘professionals-only’ approach. We therefore put together a program consisting of 160 events where exhibitors can engage with consumers outside of the Winemakers’ Dinner. From ‘Sip & Paint’ to a round-robin table tennis tournament featuring non-alcoholic wine and burlesque performances in a club, there really was something for every target group and budget. On social media, we achieved over one million impressions, almost entirely organically.

Furthermore, we work very closely with the city of Düsseldorf and Düsseldorf Tourism on an ongoing basis, and we wanted to showcase together what the city has to offer. ProWein City Vibes will be back again by popular demand in 2027!”

ProWein 2027 will debut a new exhibition format called the Discovery Zone. What can you tell us about it?

“Our Discovery Zone brings back a key function of ProWein—as a trend scout and enabler. The title says it all: we want people to unearth new and pioneering producers at ProWein. ‘Trend scouts,’ made up of external experts, writers, and critics, will search out upcoming producers and suggest them for this special zone. These companies, who need to be owner-operated and first-time ProWein exhibitors, will be able to present a total of four wines for a fixed price of €2,000. Our goal is to once again create a low-threshold entry point for innovative producers and match them in a targeted manner with international buyers. For the buyer side, the Discovery Zone offers an efficient format to both discover previously unknown products and observe developing trends in the industry.”

What other new features can attendees expect at ProWein 2027?

“There are many significant features that we are introducing in 2027, starting with moving the date of ProWein earlier to March 7 to 9 so it no longer overlaps with a major hospitality trade fair in Hamburg. We expect significantly more visitors from the restaurant/gastronomy sector, a major source of beverage sales, as a result. Successful features such as the Hosted Buyers Program and the ProWein app with its matching features are being significantly expanded. The app is also available 365 days a year and can be used for post-event interactions. Following a successful pilot project this year, ‘The Blend’ networking event will also be considerably expanded in 2027 to include partners and friends of exhibitors, Hosted Buyers, and media. Some new features are about less rather than more. We have capped the price per square meter of exhibiting to ensure a more cost-effective proposition for exhibitors. 

Together with the Sommelier Union, we will organize the first European Championship in blind wine tasting called DECODE at ProWein. This will not be a rival event to established sommelier competitions, but a pure blind tasting featuring a sophisticated and impartial IT-based scoring system. In addition to a trophy and the title of DECODER 2027, the winner will take home €5,000 and be given a spot on stage at ‘The Blend.’ We will announce the full details in due course, including how it will be complementary to the trade fair and not draw participants away from our exhibitors’ stands.”

What has changed in the wine industry since ProWein 2026?

“From an industry perspective, the pace of change has picked up. The wine and spirits industry is grappling with unprecedented social, economic, and political challenges around the world that are impacting their business directly. That is why ProWein sees itself a credible long-term partner for participants—not just during the dates of the trade fair itself but throughout the year. 

Under the ProWein Academy umbrella, our visionary talks and Agora discussions are made available online to all participants, not just those who can attend during the trade fair. And then there are global challenges such as ‘alcohol bashing,’ which require a nuanced, united response from the industry. ProWein offers various formats for exhibitors to come together and discuss important issues—both at the event itself and year-round.”

How are new generations of consumers redefining wine’s role in our society?

“With every generation, there are shifts in preferences and drinking patterns – and new generations now are no exception. There are an increasing number of studies that show younger target groups aren’t necessarily turning away from wine but often simply lack occasions to drink it. Our task is to help wine producers engage with these younger generations and to adapt their communication—and ours—n order to reach new target groups. 

‘No&low’ wines is an increasingly important category for which there is strong demand internationally, especially from younger consumers. We have responded to this demand by having a dedicated area for non-alcoholic wines, spirits and other beverages called ProWein Zero+. Our Discovery Zone meanwhile gives an opportunity for younger, less established businesses to connect with a global audience and for the visitors to see what trend-setting products have the potential to engage with a younger generation of wine drinkers.”

What trends can consumers expect to see in the coming year?

“The No&low trend will continue, with these products carving out their own space in the wine industry. I personally find the low alcohol (but still dry) wine segment (under 9% alcohol) very exciting especially since the flavor profile comes nearer to that of traditional wines. There will also be a growing demand for Proxies or alcohol-free beverages whose ingredients are similar to wine, such as grape juice or Verjus. Fresh white wines from lesser-known regions will be in focus. I see increasing segmentation within the industry from brands with a clear, consistent and stable profile to singular wines and avant-garde styles. And this is being reflected in a more sharply defined target audience for producers, who want to connect and have the tools in order to engage with those specific target groups.”

What do you hope attendees take away from ProWein 2027?

“I want exhibitors and visitors to go home saying that after more than 30 years, ProWein is still one of the most relevant dates in their business calendar. We want them to feel they have connected with the right people in Düsseldorf to create measurable value in the form of new orders and revenue streams. If we achieve this outcome, then we will consider it a success.”

title: This Retro Singapore Bar Pays Tribute to NYC’s Literary History
summary:
Cygnet Bar, the New York-themed bar in the lobby of QT Singapore, is a glamorous Art Deco throwback.

The post This Retro Singapore Bar Pays Tribute to NYC’s Literary History appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
The longest scheduled direct flight in the world is roughly 19 hours, from New York City to Singapore. You would think after traveling the length of 6.5 You Can See Everythings, I would want to experience something dramatically different than what I do at home in NYC, but as I strolled into Cygnet Bar, the elegant New York-themed bar in the lobby of QT Singapore, I saw both cities in a brand new light.

Located in one of the world’s buzziest cocktail capitals—and, within that capital, a neighborhood dense with World’s Best Bars, including Native and Jigger and Pony—Cygnet offers an invigorating POV on classic cocktail culture, through the lens of Manhattan literary history.

The Decor

The vibey, dimly lit interior at Cygnet Bar is at once glam and nostalgic, with nods to both mid-century Manhattan design and Singapore’s colonial architecture. The seating is plush and intimate, and leather-lined dining booths create a semi-private feel for small groups. The glowing backlit bar—Cygnet Bar’s focal point—features curving, ribbed mirrors that make the Art Deco-inflected space feel expansive and a little bit opulent.

The Drinks

Named after important works in New York City literary history—as well as the “iconic writing showcased at the New York Public Library,” the menu states—Cygnet Bar’s signature drinks riff on American classic cocktails. Just Kids, named after the Patti Smith memoir, is an intriguing, supremely sippable Gin Fizz riff made with Seven Tails spiced brandy, Amontillado sherry, and Foamee, a creamy vegan alternative to egg whites. Up in the Old Hotel, a nod to the Joseph Mitchell collection, is a smoky Old Fashioned twist with Fernet and Amaro Lucano. Kye Seng Ang, Cygnet Bar’s Venue Manager, calls the latter “familiar, but made for lingering.”

The spot’s bracing signature martini—the Cygnet QT-ini—features Welsh Cygnet gin (no relation), red onion brine, and Mancino vermouth. It makes the perfect pairing for the bar’s seaweed fries, lobster roll, or just about any of the American comfort food-inspired bites. The No & Low Section of the menu is impressive, too, with a nice selection of zero-proof wines (including Plus or Minus Pinot Noir from Australia, where the QT hotel brand is based) and cocktails like the juniper-forward Non Collins.

The Crowd

As a solo sipper, I felt comfortable in my little booth reading a book and enjoying my jet-lagged happy hour alone, but there were plenty of small groups enjoying a post-work drink. In fact, most patrons didn’t seem to be staying at the hotel at all. (I was very lucky that I was: the rooms are spacious and well-designed.) To me, there’s no better endorsement of a hotel bar than when it is bustling with locals meeting up with locals. 

I visited Cygnet Bar before dinner, and the energy was buzzing but certainly not rowdy. When I returned from dinner, I spotted a few couples enjoying digestivi.

The Bottom Line

For a taste of one of the most expensive cities in the world (NYC) in another famously expensive city (Singapore), the prices are quite reasonable—cocktails hover in the $18 USD area, and a great happy hour special slashes that number in half for a rotating selection of drinks. (All classic cocktails are around $12 during that 5 pm to 8 pm window, with more deals on snacks.)

With fair prices and a glam retro atmosphere, Cygnet Bar is a chic (but unfussy) cocktail bar making genuinely excellent drinks. Is it worth flying 19 hours around the world? Possibly, if you consider the fact it sits directly next to Lau Pa Sat’s Satay Street, a magical block of open-air grilled skewer vendors.

title: Our New World Winery of the Year Is an Argentine Wine Pioneer
summary:
Bodegas Salentein has set a new standard for winemaking and culinary tourism in Argentina’s Uco Valley.

The post Our New World Winery of the Year Is an Argentine Wine Pioneer appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Bodegas Salentein, a pioneer in Argentina’s Uco Valley, has played a significant role in promoting the region on the world stage while investing in its development. Founded in the late 1990s by Dutch entrepreneur Mijndert Pon, the family-owned winery honors Pon’s entrepreneurial spirit and vision by focusing on site expression and sustainability.

The Uco Valley is a relatively new wine region in Mendoza. Old vineyards exist in the valley’s lower parts, but only three decades ago did producers begin to see the potential of the higher-altitude sites. Mijndert Pon was the first to invest heavily there, planting Malbec vines in 1997 and building a state-of-the-art winery at an elevation of nearly 4,000 feet the following year. 

“He wanted to help unlock the potential of an extraordinary region and share it with the world,” says his daughter, Frederike Pon, who now runs the winery with her brother, Ben.

Frederike and Ben carry his vision forward by continuing to evolve the Uco Valley while upholding Bodegas Salentein’s core values: “Respect for the land, commitment to quality, and a belief that the best is still ahead of us,” explains Frederike.

That commitment to quality, paired with decades of research and a deep understanding of the valley, results in delicious wines across their portfolio. Entry-level and mid-tier brands like Portillo, Killka, and Reserve offer an approachable, enjoyable introduction to the region’s style. Highly scored premium wines like Numina, Single Vineyard, Pr1mum, and Gran VU Blend are made from selected vineyards, highlighting site expression.

“Our philosophy is simple,” she says, “every wine should honestly express its origin and deliver exceptional value within its category.”

Salentein’s Single Vineyard wines, which hail from the sought-after San Pablo sub-region, reflect that philosophy. The producer recognized its potential early and was instrumental in establishing it as a Geographical Indication.

Building the winery shortly after planting its first vineyards allowed Bodegas Salentein to produce and bottle on-site, showing a long-term commitment to the region. It also opened the first lodge and later launched Killka-Espacio Salentein, a space that combines wine, art, gastronomy, and hospitality—and set the standard for wine tourism in the area.

Other key aspects of their work include responsible water management and biodiversity conservation. They also prioritize access to education, support transportation for children in remote parts of the Uco Valley, and partner with organizations focused on housing, health, food security, and social inclusion.

The same foundation behind this work has made Bodegas Salentein a leader in Argentine wine. A legacy born at the intersection of nature and craftsmanship that, nearly three decades later, continues to define the region.

title: Why a Former Emergency Physician Is Wine Enthusiast’s Innovator of the Year
summary:
Dr. Laura Catena, of Bodega Catena Zapata, is a leader in old-vine preservation, soil research, and no- and low-alcohol wines.

The post Why a Former Emergency Physician Is Wine Enthusiast’s Innovator of the Year appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Many people get into wine after successful careers in other fields, making the industry richer and more diverse. But more importantly, they keep it alive and ever-evolving. Dr. Laura Catena, a former emergency physician in California for nearly three decades, author, and the managing director of her family’s Argentine winery, Catena Zapata, shows that pushing boundaries often requires seeing the world through a different lens. 

Her vision and unwavering dedication to Argentine wines and the broader wine industry are among the many reasons why Wine Enthusiast is recognizing Dr. Catena with the Innovator of the Year Wine Star Award.

With degrees from Harvard and Stanford, Dr. Catena brings analytical precision to the business and leads innovative initiatives in soil research, winemaking, sustainability, and moderate wine consumption.

Much of this work starts at the Catena Institute of Wine, which she founded in 1995 to elevate Argentine wine. Some of its published and ongoing research explores soil microbiomes, preserving vine genetic diversity, old vines, the impact of high-altitude terroir, climate change, water management, and the development of no- and low-alcohol wines.

While Dr. Catena’s love for science influences her methodical approach to winemaking, as a fourth-generation vintner, she also believes tradition gives the industry something worth preserving.

“Science and innovation give us the tools to preserve what previous generations created while finding new ways to express our region,” she says. Her visionary leadership has earned numerous awards and high scores for Catena Zapata wines, as well as for her own wineries, Luca and Domaine Nico. She has also been recognized for her efforts in safeguarding old vines.

Dr. Catena also created In Defense of Wine, a website that explains the latest science on alcohol and health, solidifying her status as a leading expert on moderating wine consumption. The Catena Institute of Wine also developed Domaine EdeM, a line of no- and low-alcohol wines. This ambitious project combined sensory analysis knowledge, human panel data, and cutting-edge technology; she believes they will “someday compete with some of the best classic wines.” 

Along with her son Dante McDermott Catena, who also works on Domaine EdeM, she launched the Zebra Striping Podcast, an interview series with industry experts that explores the emerging trend of alternating between alcoholic and non-alcoholic wines. 

“I am very proud of all this, because after all, I am a doctor and I want people to be healthy,” she says, “but I also want them to experience pleasure and spend many beautiful moments socializing at the table with friends and family, and that is where wine’s most important role is.”

title: Our Importer of the Year Puts Family-Run Producers First
summary:
Ten years ago, Francesco Ganz decided that Italian wine deserved way more than a single line in an importer’s catalog.

The post Our Importer of the Year Puts Family-Run Producers First appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Ten years ago, Francesco Ganz was convinced that Italian wine deserved way more than a single line in an importer’s catalog. The category deserved a champion. Today, that conviction and dedication have earned Ethica Wines the 2026 Wine Star Award for Importer of the Year.

Ganz grew up in the Veneto Dolomites, visiting wineries with his father and learning that wine is inseparable from the people and places behind it. He founded Ethica Wines to stand with Italian producers as a true partner, not just an importer. 

To help bring his vision to life, an executive team joined him at Ethica. Paolo Bressan, VP of Sales Off-Trade, came up through the cellar with harvests in Sicily, California, and Veneto. Damiano Sorato, VP of Sales On-Trade, spent 15 years as a sommelier in Michelin-starred restaurants across four countries. Paola Lena, CFO, brought the financial discipline the business demanded. And Lara Lona, Logistics and Purchasing Director, has been the operational backbone from nearly the beginning. “We started with a clear vision: to bring sales, marketing, logistics, and operations under one roof,” says Ganz. 

Why Italy? The answer goes well beyond heritage. Italy is a country of many singular, irreducible identities, where a region’s culture, cuisine, and landscape can feel like an entirely different world from the next, and where a single hillside or village can produce something that exists nowhere else. That sense of place makes Italy not just a category but an endless conversation. 

“Italy offers a complete world of wine within one country,” Ganz says. “Unmatched diversity, centuries of history, native varieties, distinctive territories, and an endless capacity for discovery.”

The company’s name reflects its character: Guided by a sense of integrity, Ethica’s foundation rests on the relationships between family-run producers and the people who represent them every day. “We choose winery partners who share our ambition to build brands, relationships, and lasting value,” Ganz says. Their bottles carry “the history, beauty, ambition, and work of generations.”

The Wine Star Award arrives as Ethica Wines turns 10. Ganz is the first to share the credit. “It recognizes the company and, above all, the employees, winery partners, distributors, customers, and industry professionals who have built this journey with us.”

title: Our European Winery of the Year Made Champagne What It Is Today
summary:
Bernard de Nonancourt led Champagne Laurent-Perrier with innovation and curiosity. Today, his daughters carry on the tradition.

The post Our European Winery of the Year Made Champagne What It Is Today appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
“There are two keys to success: the quality of people and the quality of wines.” That was Bernard de Nonancourt’s philosophy and the guiding light of Champagne Laurent-Perrier after he took over the Tours-sur-Marne house in 1948. Later generations have continued to honor his credo, building it into their DNA.

De Nonancourt envisioned a refreshing Champagne style exuding purity and elegance. He pioneered stainless-steel vinification, a method that shaped the bright and precise character of the wines. In 1959, when single-vintage wines were the norm, he bucked the trend and launched Grand Siècle, a prestige cuvée assembled from exceptional years to recreate the “perfect expression.” A decade later came Cuvée Rosé, made through the maceration of Pinot Noir, a demanding method for a rare style. His deep knowledge of the vineyards led him to pioneer the Ultra Brut style, which gave rise to the non-dosage category.

“Each of these choices reflects the unique savoir-faire of Laurent-Perrier,” says his daughter, Alexandra Pereyre de Nonancourt, “and continues to guide us as we shape the house’s present and future.” 

Today, Alexandra and her sister, Stéphanie Meneux de Nonancourt, lead the Maison with conviction and curiosity. “Innovation at Laurent-Perrier has always been at the service of our wines,” Stéphanie says. “Our father taught us to question the ordinary while honoring the people, terroir, and traditions that came before us.” 

This spirit comes through clearly in the glass. With the non-vintage cuvées, Grand Siècle, and the new Héritage Brut cuvée, the wines share a signature of precision and finesse that makes the house style instantly recognizable.

“This recognition from Wine Enthusiast belongs to the entire Laurent-Perrier family,” Stéphanie says, crediting the growers who tend the vineyards, the chefs de cave and winemaking team, and the house’s partners in the United States who share its story with passion.

The sisters are honored to dedicate the Wine Star Award to their father’s memory, hoping it will inspire the next generation to carry forward his spirit of innovation and challenging conventions. Stéphanie emphasizes the importance of “always staying true to the fundamental values that define us, and above all, our unwavering commitment to the quality of our wines.”

title: Our Environmental Advocate of the Year Has Always Been Ahead of the Curve
summary:
Benziger Family Winery, a biodynamic pioneer in Sonoma, remains committed to healthier vines and better wines.

The post Our Environmental Advocate of the Year Has Always Been Ahead of the Curve appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Long before “organic” was a buzzword, Benziger Family Winery was blazing the trail. 

In the mid-’90s, if you had asked an American wine drinker what biodynamic farming was, you’d likely get a blank stare, or potentially an answer about manure and a horn. Nowadays, you’re more than likely to hear about thoughtful farming practices that include sheep, cover crops, and balance with nature—not to mention delicious wines. 

Wine has come a long way since then, and so has Benziger. 

The Benziger family purchased their ranch on Sonoma Mountain in 1980, and soon recognized that the land they lived on and farmed wasn’t responding well to the conventional practices of the time. The soils were sparse, wildlife was all but absent, and the quality of the fruit they produced was underwhelming. It became clear to the family that they needed to make changes.

Biodynamic farming let them treat their vineyard and the surrounding land as one healthy, connected ecosystem. The Benzigers also recognized the potential to make even better wines from healthier vines. By the mid-’90s, Benziger had fully committed to biodynamic principles, with certification coming a few years later, in 2000. 

“What makes me most proud is that the values my family built Benziger on continue to thrive today,” says vintner Chris Benziger. “Our commitment to caring for the land, farming responsibly, and leaving our vineyards better than we found them has remained unchanged.”

Since then, the brand has evolved, with a new generation taking the reins after Mike Benziger’s retirement, new vineyards coming on line, and new ownership in 2015 by The Wine Group. But everything that’s happened since those early transition years has continued Benziger’s longstanding commitment to environmentally focused practices in the vineyard and beyond. 

Chris Benziger, Director of Winemaking Lisa Amaroli, and Vineyard Manager Jerry Mackling work tirelessly to improve the quality of the wine in the bottle and expand their vision for truly sustainable viticulture beyond their own vineyards.

With small choices and big commitments, Benziger and The Wine Group have shown that a focus on the environment and on the vine can go hand in hand, paving the way toward a more sustainable future.

title: Our American Winery of the Year Is Ground Zero for California Chardonnay
summary:
Few estates in the history of Sonoma wine have done more to refine and elevate New World Chardonnay than Chalk Hill.

The post Our American Winery of the Year Is Ground Zero for California Chardonnay appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Over half a century ago, Fred Furth founded a 1,300-acre Sonoma County estate that would become synonymous with both its appellation and the rise of California Chardonnay.

The Chalk Hill appellation is a cool pocket of light, ash-rich soils tucked around the northeastern corner of the Russian River Valley. This allows Chardonnay to ripen slowly, giving the potential for wines of structure in a variety of styles.

When Bill Foley acquired Chalk Hill from Furth in 2010, he knew that the site was a powerhouse for Chardonnay, especially the rich, full-bodied style that he preferred. But a tour of the vineyards opened his eyes to both the scale of the place and the potential it held. Foley remembers his initial impressions: “I thought, this is daunting, but it’s iconic. It’s been here since the ’70s. I knew Chalk Hill and thought, if I’m looking for something distinctive that I can really make beautiful…this is probably the place.”  

Chalk Hill Estate encompasses well over a thousand acres, but less than a third is planted to vine. Courtney Foley finds this balance to be crucial to the final product and has no plans to meaningfully change that ratio. “That mix ensures that we’re able to retain the things that make the property special ecologically, but also how that affects the way the wine tastes,” she says. 

The certified sustainable property is home to a wide range of animal life, from insects to apex predators that keep the vineyard in balance with the surrounding wildscape. And the possibilities for the estate have never been better. 

Since acquiring the property, the Foley Family Wines team has experimented tirelessly with the area’s potential for Chardonnay. From aspect, rootstock, and spacing to a wide variety of clones, including the signature Clone 97, a.k.a. the Chalk Hill clone, the group’s sole focus has been to refine and elevate the wines.

Even as they push the limits, they’ve held firm to many of the stylistic markers that built the brand’s reputation. Courtney Foley, who carried the winemaking torch for a time, notes, “We haven’t changed the style [of the estate Chardonnay] that much since David Ramey was around. We still do native fermentation. We still do sur lie aging, with weekly stirring.” 

Winemaker Darrell Holbrook has been here since the 1990s and knows every vine intimately, from subtle differences in soil composition to wind flow around the property. That type of experience allows for a high degree of specificity, and Chalk Hill has gradually expanded its offerings to include a range of styles for every Chard lover, from high-tone and fresh to opulent and rounded. 

They also offer a smaller selection of reds that have performed nicely in this tiny corner of Sonoma. But let’s be honest: This place is ground zero for Chardonnay, and everyone knows it.

title: Our RTD of the Year Proves That Chasing Trends Is Not the Answer
summary:
The Finnish Long Drink, a beloved Scandinavian RTD, traces its origins back to the 1952 Summer Olympics in Helsinki.

The post Our RTD of the Year Proves That Chasing Trends Is Not the Answer appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
If you think ready-to-drink cocktails in a can are new, think again: The Finnish Long Drink, a beloved Scandinavian RTD, traces its origins back to the 1952 Summer Olympics in Helsinki.

For those unfamiliar, a “long drink”—or “lonkero,” in Finnish—is lengthened with soda water (or another mixer) into a sessionable sipper. In this case, a mix of gin, grapefruit, and soda was developed as a refreshing cocktail to serve crowds of thirsty spectators at the Olympics. 

Yet, the drink’s popularity lingered long after the closing ceremony.

“Over the decades, it grew into one of Finland’s most beloved and iconic beverage categories,” says Phil Rosse, CEO of The Mark Anthony Group of Companies, which acquired the brand in April 2026. “In 2018, a group of Finnish and American entrepreneurs introduced their version of this longstanding Finnish tradition to the U.S. market.”

The drink, usually sold in eye-catching turquoise cans, attracted celebrities like actor Miles Teller and Norwegian record producer Kygo to become early investors.

That backing helped the brand grow at a rapid clip: The Finnish Long Drink has tripled in size since 2022, moving 3.3 million nine-liter cases in 2025, making it the sixth-largest spirit-based RTD in the U.S. 

“The results speak for themselves,” Rosse says. “The Finnish Long Drink has grown from a niche import inspired by a beloved Finnish beverage tradition into one of the fastest-growing ready-to-drink brands in the country.”

At a time when RTDs are growing exponentially, it’s particularly remarkable that a brand has captured such market share. Even more notable is that this isn’t a shiny-new concept generating all this excitement, but one that will be celebrating 75 years since its inception in 2027.

Today, the RTD market’s evolution means consumers are making more intentional choices about what they drink and what they want from the experience, Rosse explains. Flavor, quality, and drinks that fit the occasion are valued; so is authenticity.

“That creates room for brands with a really clear point of view,” he says. “Long Drink is a good example: It has a distinctive taste and a story that comes from somewhere real, but it also fits naturally into the way people are drinking today.” 

While innovation across flavors and formats will continue (see: zero sugar, flavored, and higher-proof options), the plan is to continue to build on what makes the brand different, “rather than chasing every trend.”

title: Winemaker of the Year Paolo Saracco Redefined an Entire Category
summary:
Saracco sparked a Moscato movement that changed how Americans drink, all from a hilltop in Piedmont.

The post Winemaker of the Year Paolo Saracco Redefined an Entire Category appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Paolo Saracco accomplished what many in the wine world had deemed impossible. He took a wine thought to be simple and turned it into one of the most beloved styles in the world. 

Saracco sparked a Moscato movement that changed how Americans drink. He did it all from a hilltop in Piedmont, driven by optimism and a fierce belief in a single grape variety. That’s why Wine Enthusiast is honored to name Saracco the 2026 Winemaker of the Year. 

Saracco was raised in the village of Castiglione Tinella, steeped in the region’s wine-growing and winemaking tradition. He graduated from the prestigious Alba School of Enology and returned home to take over the family estate. Where others might have played it safe and followed generations of tradition, he made a bold decision: to bottle wine grown only in his family’s vineyards, put his own name on the label, and introduce Moscato d’Asti to the world on his own terms.

That bet paid off, but not without plenty of sacrifice and travel to retail shops and restaurants around the world to promote artisanal Moscato d’Asti. Through sheer perseverance, and with the help of a group of dedicated importers, Paolo Saracco Moscato d’Asti took off. 

Saracco’s neighbors in Asti saw his success, and soon other wineries started making Moscato d’Asti with the same forethought he put into his vines and wines. No longer would Moscato d’Asti be a fizzy, simple wine; it would be a delicious wine that showed off the grape, the territory, and its people. Saracco brought an entire wine category to life.

One would think that this success would lead him to slow down, but there is no chance; today, 95% of his vineyards are planted with Moscato Bianco. He has doubled down on Moscato d’Asti and its future. 

Saracco wants people to understand that Moscato d’Asti is not just a guilty pleasure. It is a wine of elegance, freshness, and depth. He is just getting started
